sources.text: Daytime sky is blue because nitrogen/oxygen molecules (much smaller than visible wavelengths) Rayleigh-scatter short-wavelength blue light much more strongly than long-wavelength red light.
Rayleigh scattering intensity scales approximately as 1/lambda^4, so blue (~400-450 nm) is scattered several times more efficiently than red (~650-700 nm).

The sky looks blue rather than violet because sunlight contains less violet, upper-atmosphere absorption removes some violet, human eyes are less sensitive to violet than blue, and red+green cone responses blend scattered violet/indigo toward pale blue.

Sunsets/sunrises look red/orange because the low sun's light takes a much longer path through the atmosphere, so most blue/violet has been scattered away and mainly longer red-yellow wavelengths reach the eye directly.

Gas molecules cause wavelength-selective Rayleigh scattering (blue sky), while larger dust, pollution, salt, smoke and cloud droplets cause weakly wavelength-dependent Mie scattering that whitens the sky/haze and can intensify red sunsets.
The scattering explanation is named for Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt, 1842-1919), who published the theory in 1871 with elaborations through the 1880s-1890s.
